title: The house is the place of practice
hookLine: Shiva tells the goddess how a busy householder walks the highest road
carry: the householder's every act, offered to Brahman
tomorrow: why would worship start by touching your own body?
last: A MERCY FOR A HURRIED AGE.

lines: SIX A.M., THREE JOBS AT ONCE.
THE PATH, OR IN THE WAY?
cards: Six in the morning, and a dad is already three things at once: packing a lunch, listening to his mother on speaker, hunting for a lost shoe. Someone knocks. A neighbor needs a hand.
His coffee goes cold on the counter. Is this the spiritual life, or the thing keeping him from it?
The Mahanirvana Tantra stops, in the middle of Shiva's answer to the goddess, to describe this man: a grihastha, a householder.

teach.h: PARVATI: HOW, IN A HURRIED AGE?
teach.b: Here's the story behind it. In the Mahanirvana Tantra, the goddess Parvati asks Shiva a worried question: in this hard, hurried age, how will ordinary people, busy and short of time, reach the highest?
Part of his answer is a portrait of a grihastha, a householder.
He is devoted to Brahman, the highest reality, and still fully at home. He works, and works honestly. He keeps his speech truthful.
He honors his mother and father, and the text treats them as gods a person can actually see. He cares for his spouse and his children. Guests are welcomed, not tolerated.
And the thread through all of it: whatever he does, he offers to Brahman. This is a big teaching of Hinduism, not just of one book.

teach.h: ONE OF FOUR STAGES OF LIFE.
teach.b: The householder's life is one of the four classic stages of life, and the old law books praise it as the stage the others lean on, the way living things lean on the air.
The monk is honored on this path; so is the parent packing a lunch. So the cold coffee has its answer.
The duties of an ordinary day, offered, aren't a detour on the way to the highest; they're part of the road. Some readers hear an echo of the Bhagavad Gita: whatever you do, offer it.
Tantra has a reputation for the forbidden and the secret.

teach.h: A LUNCHBOX AND AN OPEN DOOR.
teach.b: Here it is in a lunchbox and an open door.

how: Some Hindu families in tantric and Shakta lineages see household duties as part of their practice, and teachers draw on the Mahanirvana Tantra's householder chapters when they speak about family life.

games.q: what does “what tantra actually is” mean?
o: a householder's ordinary day, offered, as the road
a rite done once a year for the whole household
leaving home for a forest hut to find the highest

games.q: the householder, by the book. tap the pairs.

s: in the Mahanirvana Tantra, a householder must leave home to reach the highest
the house itself is the place of practice; every act is offered to Brahman.
the text treats mother and father as gods a person can see
honoring them is part of the householder's road.

games.q: your friend says she'll start her spiritual life once her kids are grown and the house is quiet. what does the Mahanirvana's householder suggest?
o: the house is already the place of practice, every act offered.
she's right: family duties are a detour from the highest.
she should step away now; real practice needs a quiet cave.
games.why: Shiva's householder works, cares for parents, spouse, children and guests, and offers all of it to Brahman. nobody is sent to a cave.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for part of the sit, to a sink, a door or a window, as if the walk itself were an offering.
If you're staying put, rest your hands open and bring to mind one ordinary task waiting today, offered before it's begun.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, a path the Mahanirvana Tantra lays through a householder's day, every act offered.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one who stands in the house; a householder.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: the householder's every act, offered to Brahman. A lunchbox can be worship. Day sixteen-eighteen.

sources.ref: Mahanirvana Tantra, chapter 8 (the householder's duties: devotion to Brahman, honest work, truthful speech, honoring mother and father, care for spouse and children, welcoming guests, offering every act to Brahman)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 (whatever you do, offer it)
Manusmriti 3.77-78 (as living things depend on air, the other stages of life depend on the householder)
